passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. Twenty healthy adults aged 20-30 were recruited and randomly assigned to either a caffeine group (200 mg) or a placebo group. Each participant completed a computerized visual reaction time task consisting of 100 trials. The task required pressing a button as soon as a target stimulus appeared on the screen. Researchers recorded the reaction time (RT) for each trial and calculated the mean RT for each participant. The data were then aggregated by group. Table 1 summarizes the mean RTs and standard deviations for the caffeine and placebo groups. The study aimed to determine whether caffeine ingestion leads to a statistically significant improvement in reaction time compared to placebo.
stem: Which group demonstrated the faster mean reaction time according to Table 1?

options.C: Both groups had identical mean RTs
options.D: The table does not provide mean RTs

explanation: The caffeine group had a mean RT of 310 ms, which is lower (faster) than the placebo group's 350 ms.
trap: Some students may mistakenly think a higher mean RT indicates faster performance.

stem: Which design feature most directly balances known and unknown participant characteristics between the caffeine and placebo groups?

options.A: Random assignment to caffeine or placebo
options.B: Use of a computerized reaction time task

explanation: Random assignment distributes known and unknown participant characteristics evenly across groups on average, reducing selection bias and confounding. (Expectancy effects are controlled by the placebo and blinding, which are not listed.)
trap: Students may incorrectly choose the computerized task as the bias control, overlooking random assignment.

stem: What percent improvement in mean reaction time does caffeine produce relative to placebo?
explanation: Correct: B) (350 - 310)/350 x 100 = 11.4%. Why the others are wrong: A) 10.7% does not correspond to the correct baseline calculation. C) 12.5% is not 40 divided by either mean. D) 12.9% divides 40 by the caffeine mean (310) instead of the placebo baseline.
trap: Dividing the 40 ms difference by the caffeine mean (40/310 = 12.9%) instead of the placebo baseline, which gives option D.

stem: Which statement reflects a common misinterpretation of the study’s results?

options.A: Caffeine causes a clinically significant speed‑up in all tasks.
options.B: The caffeine group had a lower mean reaction time than the placebo group.
options.C: Random assignment helps balance participant characteristics across groups.
options.D: The standard deviations of the two groups (45 ms and 50 ms) are similar in size.

explanation: Option A overgeneralizes: the study measured one reaction-time task in a small sample of healthy adults, so it cannot show a clinically significant speed-up in all tasks. Options B, C, and D are accurate statements.
trap: Students may think the reduction is clinically meaningful without evidence of broader applicability.

stem: Which feature of the study most limits applying its findings to shift workers?

options.A: Participants were healthy adults aged 20-30 tested in a laboratory on a single visual reaction-time task.
options.B: Participants were randomly assigned to caffeine or placebo.
options.C: Each participant’s mean reaction time was calculated from 100 trials.
options.D: A placebo group was included for comparison.

explanation: Correct: A) Shift workers differ from healthy young adults tested in a lab on one task, so the setting, population and task limit generalization. Why the others are wrong: B) Random assignment strengthens internal validity and does not limit generalization to workers. C) Averaging 100 trials makes each participant’s mean more reliable. D) Including a placebo group improves the comparison and is not a limitation.
trap: Treating a strength of the design (randomization or a placebo group) as the reason results may not apply to shift workers.
